title: Don't despair
hook: O My servants who have wronged yourselves, don't despair of Allah's mercy, He forgives all sins (39:53)

segments.voice: Yesterday, lubb, the kernel at the core of ulu'l-albab, and your line was knowing isn't equal to not knowing. Did you find ten minutes to read? Day five hundred fifty-nine.

A group of men come to the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ. They've done terrible things: killed many times, and committed adultery many times. They've listened to his message, and they like it. But they have one problem, and they say it straight. What you're calling us to is good. If only you could tell us there's a way to make up for what we've done. They aren't arguing. They're asking whether it's already too late. A report in Sahih al-Bukhari says the answer came as revelation, and one of the verses was this one.

Surah Az-Zumar, verse fifty-three. Pickthall: "Say: O My slaves who have been prodigal to their own hurt! Despair not of the mercy of Allah, Who forgiveth all sins. Lo! He is the Forgiving, the Merciful." Start with the address. Ya 'ibadiya, O My servants. Before a word about what they did, Allah calls them His. People who have gone too far, the Arabic says, against their own souls, and they're still addressed as Mine. And the first command isn't to do this or that. It's: don't despair. La taqnatu. The verb names the despair of someone who has stopped expecting anything. The verse forbids that before it promises anything else. Then the promise: He forgives all sins, jami'an, every one of them. Scholars read this together with the very next verse, which says: turn to your Lord and submit to Him before the punishment comes. So the door is wide, and the way through it is turning back. Some early authorities are reported to have called it the most hopeful verse in the Qur'an. And notice who it was for. Not people with small slips, but men who had killed. Teachers draw the point out: if the verse reached them, it reaches the person who skipped their prayers for a month, or broke a promise, or fell back into an old habit. In that reading, the danger isn't only the mistake. It's deciding the mistake is the end.

The practice: come back after a lapse. Sit, and think of one good habit you let slip: a prayer, a walk, a call to a parent, this very path if you missed some days. Notice any voice saying it's too late, or you always do this. Hear the verse's first words instead: O My servants. Then decide the smallest way to come back today. Not to make up for everything. Just to return. If you pray, you can say astaghfirullah. The bell holds the time.
Don't despair. Az-Zumar fifty-three: to people who have wronged themselves, never lose hope in Allah's mercy, for He forgives all sins to those who turn back. Today's word.
Your line: never despair of mercy. Today, pick up the habit you let slip, even for one minute, without making up for the gap. Day five hundred fifty-nine.

howItsDone: Muslims seek forgiveness by saying astaghfirullah, often many times a day, and many scholars and preachers quote 39:53 to people who feel their sins are too great to be forgiven.

myth: the verse was revealed for people with only small sins
a report in Bukhari says it answered men who had killed and done worse.
the verse calls wrongdoers My servants before anything else
ya 'ibadiya: they're addressed as His first.
scholars read the verse together with a call to turn back
the next verse says: turn to your Lord and submit to Him.

fork.setup: men who had done terrible things tell the Prophet: your message is good, but is there any way back for us? what came in answer?
options: first, make up for every wrong.
fork.reveal: don't despair of Allah's mercy: He forgives all sins, with the next verse asking them to turn back to Him.

original.note: Arabic: don't despair, from the root q-n-t, the despair of someone who stops expecting anything.

trapdoor: what you thought: some sins are too big to forgive.
what it means: people who wronged themselves are still called His servants, and told never to despair.
what a scholar hears: 39:53's occasion is reported in Bukhari 4810; jami'an is read with 39:54's call to repentance, and some early authorities called it the most hopeful verse.

sources.quoted: Say: O My slaves who have been prodigal to their own hurt! Despair not of the mercy of Allah, Who forgiveth all sins. Lo! He is the Forgiving, the Merciful.

notes: Pickthall wording of 39:53 quoted from memory; please confirm.
Bukhari 4810 (polytheists who had killed asking about expiation; 25:68 and 39:53 revealed) cited from memory; confirm.
'Most hopeful verse' attributed to Ibn 'Abbas and others; attributions vary in tafsir (some cite 'Ali or Ibn Mas'ud). Confirm.
Scholars read 'all sins' with 39:54 (repentance) and 4:48 (shirk without repentance); the script mentions only 39:54.

Editor review: hook now follows Bukhari 4810's wording (killed and committed adultery much) instead of 'and worse', and drops the unsourced 'in Mecca'; 'most hopeful verse' is now 'some early authorities are reported to' (attribution varies); removed the transliteration 'qunut', which collides with qunut (devotion/the night-prayer supplication); narrator's theological conclusion reframed as what teachers draw out.
